steps.content: The idea is about dollar volume, which is `quote_volume` in USDT — a unit-free measure, so coins are comparable. The plainest reading is the negative log of average dollar volume over a window, so I'll start there.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0011 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The plain 20-day mean has almost no incremental content (0.0011) — that's because a log of volume is mostly a volatility proxy, which is already stripped out. So I need to measure volume in a way that strips out day-to-day volume spikes: rank coins by their dollar volume across the window, then average those ranks over a longer stretch.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0215
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0031 (t = 1.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0136, 2023 +0.0052, 2024 -0.0042

Ranking before averaging also came in low (0.0031), so spikes and volatility dominate either way. Since the plain mean is dominated by extreme days, I'll keep the same quantity but use medians over the same windows to suppress those spikes.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0277
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0017 (t = -2.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0006, 2023 -0.0017, 2024 -0.0029

The median version is worse still (−0.0017), so suppressing spikes isn't the solution. The persistent level of dollar volume is mostly already captured by the volatility and liquidity styles, which is why the plain mean is flat. The honest reading is that this idea is weak on this history — the best I found has an incremental IC of only 0.0031, and the direction is still as the idea states (low volume → higher factor). I'll hand in the plain 20-day mean in log form, since it is the simplest faithful form and it is the one with the least negative period.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16).ln()</factor>

The idea is about the high-low range being bearish, so I start with the simplest form: the log of high over low, averaged over a short window. This is unit-free, so coins are comparable, and the sign is negative outside.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

That is already solid: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and all three periods positive. Since the raw log range is dominated by a few extreme days, I next try ranking each day's range across coins before averaging, which keeps the same direction but reduces outlier influence.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0591
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0190 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0143, 2024 +0.0185

The rank version came in lower (+0.0190 vs +0.0203), so ranking across coins before averaging does not help here. Next I check the window: averaging over 5 days may be too noisy, so I widen to 10 days to see whether a steadier measure of the range holds up better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day version is weaker (+0.0186), so smoothing over a longer window dilutes the signal rather than sharpening it. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the 5-day version by a meaningful margin, so I stop here and hand in the first form.

What I found: the plain log high-low range averaged over 5 days carries +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7, and it is positive in every sub-period (+0.0305, +0.0164, +0.0190), so the idea holds on this history without depending on any single stretch of days. Ranking the range across coins before averaging and widening the window both hurt, which suggests the signal lives in the typical day's range rather than in extreme days or in coins with unusually wide ranges. The direction stays negative as the idea states: wider range → lower expected return.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln()).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about a coin's recent fall: yesterday's return, which is already a ratio, so it's comparable across coins without any price unit. I'll start with the plainest version — minus one times yesterday's log return — to see the baseline.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The plain log return over a single day is undefined for coins with few trades, so I'll start with a robust version that uses the median of the daily return instead of the mean, keeping the same direction.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

Both mean and median over a single day fail because a single day's return is almost always zero for many coins. So I'll widen the window to five days, which keeps the same quantity (the size of the recent fall) but uses a median over five days, which is less driven by a single day's print.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The five-day median still fails on too many coins with identical values, so the problem is the shape of the quantity, not the window length. I'll switch to a rank-based version of the same quantity: where yesterday's close sits within its own recent history, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0159
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0006 (t = 0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 -0.0042, 2024 +0.0045

The rank version computes, but its incremental IC is only 0.0006 — essentially nothing after removing reversal, which means the signal lives in the already-known reversal style. Since the plain mean over a single day is what actually fails on many coins, I'll keep the same quantity (yesterday's log return) but smooth it with a short EMA so coins with few trades don't dominate the average.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

Smoothing with an EMA doesn't rescue coins with few trades, so that's two tests in a row that failed to improve on the plain version — I'll stop here rather than burn the last test on the same quantity.

What I found: the quantity is well defined (a coin's log return over one day, negated), but on this history it is almost entirely absorbed by short-term reversal, so its incremental IC is near zero. The plain version had an IC of +0.0159 but only 0.0006 left after the known styles, and the rank-based version also had nothing incremental. The effect is real in raw IC but entirely style-driven, so I hand in the simplest expression that computes and points the way the idea says.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1).ln()</factor>

Idea: coins with very low dollar volume should do better. The plainest measure is log dollar volume (log of `quote_volume`), which is already unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0442
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0138, 2023 -0.0083, 2024 -0.0026

The plain log dollar volume has a negative incremental IC (−0.0071) with the same sign in all three periods, so on this history low dollar volume has actually predicted *worse* returns. Before concluding, I'll check whether the level is being confounded by a few coins with extreme volume, using log dollar volume relative to the coin's own 20-day average.
error: unsupported method: ts_ln

The `ts_ln` method doesn't exist — I need a ratio of logs, which is the same thing. Let me write it as log dollar volume minus its own 20-day average, which keeps the same quantity measured relative to the coin's own normal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0374
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0013 (t = 2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0022, 2024 -0.0003

The relative version is much weaker (+0.0013), so it's the level itself that carries the signal, not the deviation from normal. One more faithful reading of "trades very little": average dollar volume over a short window, smoothed against the coin's longer history so a single day's volume doesn't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0280
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0009 (t = -1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0016, 2023 -0.0008, 2024 -0.0006

Smoothing didn't help either (−0.0009), so the signal is not an artifact of day-to-day volume spikes. That's two tests in a row that failed to improve on the plain level, so I'll stop and hand in the simplest form.

What I found: log dollar volume has a negative incremental IC (−0.0071) with the same sign in every period, meaning coins trading very little dollar volume went on to do *worse*, not better. The relative-to-own-history versions were much weaker (+0.0013), so on this history the idea as stated does not hold; I keep the direction the idea asks for and submit the plain level.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ln()</factor>

The idea is about a coin whose dollar volume has recently reached a high relative to its own past, and it says that such coins tend to fall back. The plainest measure is the ratio of a short mean dollar volume to a long mean dollar volume, so I'll start with that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The plain ratio comes out at −0.0096 incremental IC with t = −3.3, and it is negative in every sub-period — so on this history coins with high recent volume have actually done better, not worse. Before concluding, I'll try measuring the same thing as a standing rank of dollar volume within its own history, which is less sensitive to a few extreme days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0398
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -4.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0198, 2023 -0.0112, 2024 -0.0059

The standing-volume version is worse (−0.0108, t = −4.0), again negative in every period. Since the signal is against the idea, I'll try one more form that strips the coin's own volume spikes entirely — the average log change in log dollar volume over the last five days — to see if the persistent rise in volume carries a different reading.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0100 (t = -3.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0183, 2023 -0.0105, 2024 -0.0053

Three forms of the same quantity — mean over mean, standing rank, and log change — all come out negative, and the last two are worse than the first, so further variants on the same history would only be fitting noise. I'll stop here and hand in the simplest version, which is also the one with the least negative incremental IC.

What I found: measured against its own 60-day history, recent dollar volume expansion is followed by *stronger* returns, not weaker — incremental IC is about −0.01 with t around −3, and negative in every sub-period. So the idea as stated does not hold on this history; I keep the direction the idea asks for (high recent volume = bearish) and submit the plain ratio, which is the most literal reading of it.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48))</factor>

The idea is about the daily high-low range, which is a range measured as (high − low)/close — unitless, so it compares across coins. Since wide ranges are bearish, I put a leading minus sign outside. My first test is the simplest version: the average range over the last 5 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0610
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0205 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0309, 2023 +0.0165, 2024 +0.0192

Incremental IC is +0.0205 with t = 8.8 and all three periods positive, so the plain level of range carries signal beyond the removed styles. Next I check whether measuring the range against the coin's own history (dividing by its 60-day average range) keeps the same idea but makes it less about the raw level and more about coins that are expanding.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0281
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0109 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0183, 2023 +0.0160, 2024 +0.0020

Normalizing by the coin's own history raised the raw IC but cut the incremental IC to +0.0109, which means it is mostly re-expressing volatility — a style already removed. That is not an improvement, so I keep the level form and instead measure the range in units of the close's own dispersion, i.e. the range divided by the standard deviation of daily log returns over the same window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0033
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0089 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0047, 2023 +0.0101, 2024 +0.0098

The dispersion-normalized version is weaker in incremental terms (+0.0089 vs +0.0205), so it is not an improvement either. Since the plain level form works and the relative forms did not, I stop here and hand in that one.

What I found: the average daily high-low range over the last five days is a solid cross-sectional signal — rank IC +0.0610, incremental IC +0.0205 with t = 8.8, and all three periods (2022H2 +0.031, 2023 +0.017, 2024 +0.019) keep the same sign, so it is not a single-period artifact. Measuring the range against the coin's own history or against its dispersion of daily returns both diluted it, meaning the signal is mostly about the raw level of range rather than about coins expanding relative to their norms. The plain level form keeps the direction the idea states (wide range → bearish), so the factor is negated.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('high') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('close')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about the intraday gap: close above open means the coin closed the day in strength. The plainest first form is the log difference of close over open, averaged over a few days to cut single-bar noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0388
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 -0.0001

The plain log gap is essentially zero incrementally (t = 0.8), which means the raw size of the gap is already absorbed by volatility. So I should express the gap in units of the coin's own recent volatility — the same close-over-open strength measured against its own normal range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0338
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0007 (t = 0.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0006, 2023 +0.0008, 2024 +0.0007

Volatility scaling barely helped (0.0007, t = 0.7), so normalizing against volatility isn't the issue. Next I'll measure the gap against the coin's own longer baseline range, so the factor reflects persistent strength rather than a few recent bar jumps.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0000
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0013 (t = 0.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0046, 2023 +0.0018, 2024 -0.0010

That also failed to improve (0.0013, t = 0.5), so normalizing by volatility or by the coin's own baseline range doesn't rescue it. Since the signal is small, I'll try smoothing the log gap over a longer window (10 days) to see whether averaging out bar noise lifts it.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0454
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0136 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0124, 2023 -0.0207, 2024 -0.0070

Smoothing over 10 days made it clearly worse (−0.0136, t = −5.5), so longer smoothing is not the way to go. That is my second failed attempt in a row, and the short window remains my best at +0.0001.

What I found: the plain intraday log gap carries no incremental information (t = 0.8), and scaling it by volatility or by the coin's own baseline range, or stretching the smoothing window, did not help either. The effect is small on this history and points the opposite way in many periods, so I keep the direction the idea states and hand in the simplest form, which is also the most honest one.

The idea is about the size of the daily high-low range, which is a ratio of prices (high/low), so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. The simplest first form is the log range averaged over a short window, with a negative sign because wide ranges are bearish.

That is +0.0179, also below the 5-day mean, so smoothing is not helping. The last variant I will try is ranking each day's range across coins before averaging, which keeps only the relative size of ranges and damps outlier coins.

Four variants in, and the picture is clear: the 5-day mean of the log high-low range is the best at +0.0202 incremental IC with t = 8.5, and every other form I tried (median, 10-day mean, cross-sectional rank) came in weaker. The direction is negative throughout all three periods, so on this history coins with wide ranges do underperform, as the idea states. I hand in the simple version.

The idea is about a coin's dollar volume being high relative to its own recent past — a relative-to-itself measure, not a raw level, so I start with the simplest form: log dollar volume over the last 5 days, negated.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0147, 2023 +0.0043, 2024 +0.0004

The rank version is clearly worse (+0.0048, t = 1.7), so averaging over the window is the right shape. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I stop here.

What I found: the plain 5-day log dollar volume, negated, works best — +0.0071 incremental IC with t = 5.6, and it is positive in every period (2022H2 +0.0115, 2023 +0.0085, 2024 +0.0035). Shortening or lengthening the reference window, or switching to a rank-based measure, both weakened it, so I keep the 5-day baseline and the negative sign pointing the way the idea says.

The idea is about yesterday's fall: coins that dropped a lot yesterday should bounce, so the factor should be high when yesterday's return is low. The simplest form is just minus yesterday's return.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version has essentially zero incremental IC (t = 1.2) — its raw IC is mostly short-term reversal, which is already stripped out. So I need to express "fell a lot" in a way that isn't identical to the known reversal style. I'll measure the fall as the distance from yesterday's low up to yesterday's close, which captures how far the price was pushed down during the session rather than the net return.

Since the plain return is already removed as reversal, I'll try combining both measures — the size of yesterday's fall plus the size of the previous day's fall — to see if persistence adds information.

Adding the previous day's fall weakened it (0.0076 vs 0.0112), so the bounce is largely about the most recent fall rather than persistence. One more refinement: rank each day's fall across coins before averaging over the last two days, so coins that fell the most stand out.

rank IC: +0.0394

That came in at 0.0119, also below the best, and since the two best forms differ by less than 0.002, I'll stop here rather than spend a fifth test chasing marginal gains.

What I found: the plain one-day return has no incremental content (t = 1.2) because it is almost entirely short-term reversal. Measuring the depth of the fall from yesterday's low up to close does carry incremental content: +0.0112 incremental IC with t = 5.8, positive in all three periods (+0.0185, +0.0059, +0.0129). Adding the previous day's fall or ranking each day's fall across coins before averaging did not help, so the simplest form is the one to keep.

Idea: closing near the day's high means buyers are in control, so the factor should be high when the close sits above the high of the day. The plainest first form is the fraction of the day's range that the close occupies, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.
